Modular arithmetic. Modular arithmetic is a system of arithmetic for integers where numbers wrap around after reaching a certain value called the modulus. Two integers are congruent modulo n, written as a is congruent to b modulo n, if their difference is divisible by n. Modular arithmetic abstracts the idea of remainders—clock arithmetic, days of the week—into a rigorous algebraic system. It is foundational to number theory, underpins modern cryptography like RSA encryption, and enables efficient computation through the Chinese Remainder Theorem.

Here's the definition. a is congruent to b modulo n means n divides the quantity a minus b, or equivalently, a and b have the same remainder when divided by n. The integers partition into n equivalence classes modulo n, with each class containing all integers congruent to a fixed residue: zero, one, up through n minus one. Addition and multiplication modulo n follow predictable rules: a plus b modulo n equals the quantity a modulo n plus b modulo n, all modulo n. Similarly for multiplication. These operations preserve the underlying structure.

Fermat's Little Theorem is essential: if p is prime and the greatest common divisor of a and p is one, then a to the power p minus one is congruent to one modulo p. This is essential for fast exponentiation and primality testing. A modular inverse exists when a has a multiplicative inverse modulo n, written as a inverse, such that a times a inverse is congruent to one modulo n. This happens precisely when a and n are coprime.

The Chinese Remainder Theorem solves systems of congruences. If you have multiple congruences a is congruent to b sub i modulo n sub i, where the moduli are pairwise coprime, there's a unique solution modulo the product of all the moduli. This theorem enables parallel computation and is computationally powerful.

Modular arithmetic became a discipline through Carl Friedrich Gauss's Disquisitiones Arithmeticae in 1801, though clock arithmetic is ancient. In the twentieth century it became computational: fast algorithms for modular exponentiation and the Chinese Remainder Theorem enabled efficient cryptography. RSA encryption, published in 1977, uses the computational hardness of factoring large numbers in modular arithmetic. Breaking RSA requires factoring n, which seems computationally intractable for large n. This single idea secured digital commerce for decades. Beyond cryptography, modular arithmetic appears in error-correcting codes like Reed-Solomon, pseudorandom number generation, and discrete Fourier transforms.
